vignette:
She is 19 and still speaks about the summer her son nearly died as if it happened in the next room, only a few weeks ago, though it was more than a year ago now. At the time, she is barely out of adolescence herself, living with her partner and trying to make sense of motherhood while working long shifts in a warehouse. Her days are usually noisy and physical-lifting, sorting, scanning packages under bright fluorescent lights-but before the illness, she thinks of her life as demanding in a manageable way. She is tired often, but she is proud of how she keeps going.

Everything changes when her child begins to seem "off." At first it is a fever, then listlessness, then a rapid decline that she cannot explain. She takes him to appointments, then to the emergency room, and then back again as the concern deepens and the language around the illness becomes more serious. She remembers the smell of antiseptic and the constant interruptions of alarms and footsteps. She remembers learning to read the expressions on nurses' faces because no one says directly what she is afraid of hearing. When the doctors tell her the illness is life-threatening, she experiences it as a kind of split in the world: one part of her still functioning, asking questions and nodding, while another part is staring inwardly at a picture of her child not surviving.

During those days, she becomes focused and helpless at the same time. She sits beside the hospital bed, watches the monitors, and counts each breath as if counting can keep him here. She stops eating properly and drinks too much coffee. She calls relatives, updates her partner, texts between tears, then feels guilty for every moment she steps into the hallway to cry. At night she lies awake in the chair beside the bed or, when she briefly goes home, wakes to the smallest sounds, certain something is wrong. Even after the immediate crisis passes and her child stabilizes, her body does not seem to understand that the danger has lessened. Her heart pounds whenever a phone rings. She jumps at medical dramas on television, at the beep of equipment in stores, at sudden silence, which now feels as threatening as noise.

Returning to work in the warehouse is harder than she expects. The job requires speed and attention, and she finds herself distracted by intrusive images of the hospital bed and by a sharp fear that something will happen to her child while she is packing boxes on the other side of town. She checks her phone repeatedly. When she cannot answer right away, she imagines the worst. She keeps backup plans in her head-who would pick him up, which relative could drive, what signs would mean "go now"-and rehearses them even when she is trying to focus on her shift. Her supervisor notices that she startles when someone approaches from behind. She becomes tense in noisy aisles, her shoulders locked up by the end of the day.

She also begins to avoid anything that reminds her of the illness. She does not want to walk past the pediatric wing of the hospital. She changes the channel when a child is shown in a hospital bed. She avoids talking about the details with friends, partly because she does not want pity and partly because speaking about it makes the fear return too vividly. At home, she watches her child closely for any sign of tiredness or discomfort, reading ordinary colds as possible emergencies. This vigilance leaves her exhausted, but she cannot fully let it go. When he finally sleeps peacefully, she sometimes sits beside him and feels strangely unable to trust the calm.

In the months after, she notices that she is not as present with the people around her as she used to be. Her partner says she seems far away, and she knows he is right. She can be physically there-making dinner, answering texts, packing lunches-but a large part of her remains on alert, listening for bad news. She feels ashamed of how angry and frightened she becomes over small things, and she is quick to blame herself for not being stronger during the crisis. She thinks often about how close she came to losing her child, and those thoughts come with images she does not invite, like flashes she cannot turn off.

Now, as she continues with her warehouse shifts and her responsibilities at home, she functions, but with effort that others do not always see. She smiles when expected, shows up on time, and takes care of her child with fierce attention. Yet underneath, the memory of that illness still organizes her day. Even in ordinary moments-closing a box, hearing a siren, watching her child nap-she carries the sense that safety can disappear without warning, and that she is always listening for it to happen again.
